newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil CVRD sale hit by political intrigue.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil CVRD sale hit by political intrigue.

text.p: Brazil's biggest privatization, the planned sale of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, was enmeshed in political intrigue Wednesday with senators seeking control and accusations of horse-trading.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, in a bid to quash speculation he might cede to the senators and to the states in exchange for support for another of his pet projects, re-election, said giving up on the CVRD sale was not an option.
"When it needs to, the government backtracks, but this is not the case," he told reporters in the Presidential Palace.

The $10 billion CVRD sale, due to begin with a block sale of 40-45 percent of voting shares in February, had been advancing normally until Finance Minister Pedro Malan vowed last month that the proceeds would go entirely to retire internal debt.

Senators, whose states had been promised a slice of the cake for infrastructure investment in return for their support in August in killing an opposition bill that would have hampered the sell-off, screamed foul.

Congressional anger culminated Tuesday in an anti-CVRD privatization front, formed by old-guard politicians waving the banner of "national interest" and led by two of Cardoso's most constant foes, former presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco.
Fears the alliance could hamper the sell-off hit CVRD's blue chip preferred shares Wednesday, which slipped 0.89 percent in the morning.
"There is concern about this Sarney-Itamar alliance," said Sergio Missima of Fator Securities in Brazil.
Political analysts broadly dismiss the Sarney-Franco threat.

But Sarney, ambiguous as ever in his support for and constant machinations against Cardoso, suggested he might trade his opposition to a constitutional amendment allowing Cardoso's re-election for more Senate control over the CVRD sale.
That led to reports Cardoso could well concede over CVRD, a charge he denied.
"The word bargain has no place in this government," Cardoso insisted, according to the private Invest News agency.
Cardoso said the Senate could analyze the sale, but that the decision to privatize was for the executive alone to make.

The president also said the government might set up a fund for state infrastructure investment. By meeting the demand of the states, Brasilia will simply be reverting to the deal it struck in the Senate months ago.
Senators allied to the government have made it clear to Cardoso that this was the best way to thwart attempts by the Sarney-Itamar camp and the opposition to obstruct the sell-off.

"Many senators feel some of the CVRD proceeds should go to infrastructure investment in the states. That's the best way to counter opponents," an aide to the government's leader in Congress, Sen. Jose Roberto Arruda, told Reuters.

Meanwhile, with political games continuing in the Presidency and in Congress, government allies managed successfully Wednesday to prevent a vote on an opposition bill that would allow the Senate to take CVRD off the privatization list.
The bill by Workers Party deputy Jose Eduardo Dutra will be presented to the Senate Economic Affairs Committee next Tuesday.
